title: Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to locate the physical trace of a specified memory, determine whether its original information remains available after an impairment, and selectively restore access to that information. “Read” would mean identifying memory-specific content, rather than merely detecting neurons active during learning. “Repair” would mean recovering the previously learned content without teaching it again, while preserving other measured memories.

Memory-associated neuronal ensembles, often called engrams, provide experimentally accessible approximations of physical memory traces. The supplied study establishes that targeted molecular intervention in such ensembles can causally alter learned memory expression in mice. Identifying an ensemble associated with learning, however, does not establish that researchers have identified the complete physical representation of the memory or decoded its content.

Conceptual distinction: a memory that cannot currently be retrieved may still retain information in its physical substrate, whereas another impairment may destroy some of that information. The proposed capability must distinguish these situations. Restoring access to retained information and reconstructing information that has been lost are different objectives; the former does not establish the latter.

significance.text: Conditional scientific significance: identifying a particular physical trace and selectively restoring its verified learned content would provide unusually direct causal evidence connecting brain mechanisms to a specific memory. It would extend the supplied study’s proof of principle—that site-specific epigenetic regulation can influence memory expression—toward an explanation of which information a trace contains and how access to it fails.

Conditional practical significance: successful restoration could make some currently inaccessible information recoverable and could support interventions tailored to a particular memory deficit. This possibility depends on enough of the original information surviving and on an intervention reaching the relevant substrate without materially disrupting other functions. Recovering a behavioral response alone would not establish recovery of a detailed autobiographical experience.

Impact limits: selective memory restoration would not by itself constitute broad treatment of dementia. Ongoing disease, loss of tissue and impairment of other cognitive functions would remain separate problems. A computer-file repair analogy is therefore limited: identifying and influencing a memory-associated ensemble does not establish that a memory exists as a discrete, completely readable file, and no supplied evidence supports recovery of destroyed information or a particular historical ranking of the breakthrough.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing combined capability is content-specific identification, assessment of residual information and selective restoration. The supplied mouse experiment demonstrates an intervention that changes memory expression, but it does not show how to identify the complete representation of an arbitrary autobiographical memory, determine whether its information survives impairment, or restore that information selectively. The supplied record does not establish whether this combined capability remains unavailable across the entire field as of 1 November 2026.

Scientific and engineering requirements inferred from the objective include distinguishing a memory-bearing substrate from activity that merely accompanies learning or retrieval; determining which physical features carry the target content; and measuring whether that content persists after impairment. The original research describes memories as distributed, changing over time and sharing neural resources. Those are relevant proposed complications, but the supplied review does not independently substantiate their full scope, so they cannot establish a field-wide impossibility claim here.

Further inferred barriers concern intervention specificity and interpretation. A successful repair must restore the target content without relearning it, avoid changes to other measured memories, and distinguish recovery from general improvements in attention, motivation or task performance. Human translation would additionally require sufficiently precise access to the relevant cells and molecular processes, durable benefit and practical limits on unintended effects. These are requirements of the proposed capability, not achievements established by the mouse study.

current_state.text: On 29 October 2025, Coda and colleagues published “Cell-type- and locus-specific epigenetic editing of memory expression.” They combined CRISPR-based epigenetic editing with learning-associated neuronal tagging to target the Arc promoter in dentate gyrus ensembles in male mice. The experiments produced bidirectional changes in contextual fear-memory expression, supporting a causal role for site-specific epigenetic regulation in that experimental setting.

The study also demonstrated reversibility within the same animals: induction of the anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA4 negated the enhanced retention produced by the dCas9-VPR activator, with reduced freezing in the behavioral assay. This establishes reversible control of experimentally enhanced memory expression. It is not a demonstrated cycle of memory impairment followed by selective repair, and it does not establish recovery of previously inaccessible autobiographical content.

The experimental scope was one genomic site, one brain region, one memory task and male animals only. The supplied review reports no arbitrary-content decoding, no test establishing preservation of multiple other memories and no human autobiographical-memory restoration. Changes in contextual fear behavior therefore support a narrower conclusion than complete identification or reading of a memory’s physical representation.

The supplied review assessed retained HTML and PDF text as complete and untruncated, including methods and extended-data captions. Its qualitative assessment relied on textual results and captions; figures, raw data and linked statistical tables were not independently inspected. Saved supplementary artifacts in the source index do not expand that reviewed evidentiary scope. These limitations constrain independent assessment of effect magnitude and robustness without implying that the reported result is false.

Coverage limitation: the supplied freshness record is empty, so the record establishes the October 2025 result but cannot establish the field’s status through 1 November 2026 or exclude newer advances. No additional quantitative effect estimates, independent replications or human demonstrations are established by the supplied materials.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed animal milestone: independently replicated experiments should identify a physical trace associated with a specified previously learned memory, produce or characterize a defined impairment, assess whether memory-specific information persists, and restore retrieval without relearning the target content. The experimental design should distinguish recovery of the original information from new learning, cue-driven performance and a general improvement in memory or task engagement.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated animal experiments recover original memory information without relearning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed selectivity and durability tests: evaluate other memories and relevant nonmemory performance before and after intervention, use blinded assessment where feasible, and measure persistence of benefit over a stated interval. Reports should specify the memory types, impairment mechanisms, species and intervention conditions tested, together with unintended effects. Preserving the measured comparison memories would establish selectivity within that tested set; finite experiments cannot establish preservation of every memory or literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate durable selectivity among tested memories, reporting conditions and effects

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation of the reading component: behavioral restoration should be accompanied by evidence connecting the identified physical features to memory-specific information. Complete physical identification and decoding require separate validation beyond successful retrieval. A persuasive claim should state whether it identifies a useful causal subset of the trace, decodes selected content, or accounts for the complete representation; these are different levels of achievement.
completion_criteria.label: Validate memory-specific information in physical traces and state identification scope

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human milestone: with informed consent, demonstrate recovery of independently documented memories using blinded tests, durable benefit and controls against general changes in attention or memory performance. Practical evaluation should establish the intervention’s precision, unintended effects and applicability to the impairment being treated. These are proposed demonstrations, not established standards, and success with selected memories would not establish broad dementia treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Recover documented human memories with blinded testing and durable benefit

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” could help explain how memory-bearing circuits encode information and generate retrieval. NRL-04 asks for identification and repair of specified memories; a general circuit theory is broader, while selective restoration could succeed within a limited domain without such a theory.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” could improve observation of candidate memory traces and their activity. Recording alone does not establish which physical features store particular content or how to repair retrieval. NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could enable precise interventions, but delivery capability does not supply the memory-specific target or repair mechanism.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” addresses reconstruction of tissue while retaining what was learned. NRL-04 focuses on identifying and repairing particular memory traces. The objectives meet when tissue loss damages a trace, but restoring retrieval from surviving information does not demonstrate replacement of tissue or reconstruction of information that no longer survives.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-09, “Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss,” concerns prevention; NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” concerns disease control and functional recovery after disease is established. Selective memory repair could contribute to recovery in some circumstances, but neither disease prevention nor arrest follows from it. NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” addresses broader disease mechanisms rather than the content of individual memories.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-01, “A causal, predictive theory of consciousness,” may intersect with conscious recollection, but restoring a learned response does not establish an explanation of subjective experience. NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis,” and NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” overlap through neural decoding or intervention methods; their functional targets differ from reading and repairing stored memories.

Roster-based synthesis: the remaining entries retain distinct targets: spinal-cord reconnection in NRL-05; cortical visual prostheses in NRL-08; immune control and remyelination in NRL-12; acute stroke protection in NRL-13; seizure freedom in NRL-14; biological visual-pathway repair in NRL-16; and interruption of the disease process associated with chronic traumatic encephalopathy in NRL-18. Their titles do not establish a direct dependency on selective memory repair. Shared interests in preserving or restoring neural function do not make them equivalent capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved NRL-04’s identity and separated physical-trace identification, content reading, residual-information assessment and selective restoration.
change_log.reason: The concept combines distinct capabilities; causal manipulation of memory expression does not establish all of them.

change_log.reason: The inspected evidence supports the experimental basis but does not substantiate every general assertion or establish contemporary field-wide limits.

change_log.change: Expanded the October 2025 result with its publication date, Arc-promoter target, learning-tagged dentate gyrus ensembles, male-mouse scope and contextual fear task.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the useful experimental explanation while defining the limits of generalization.

change_log.change: Clarified that anti-CRISPR reversed experimentally enhanced retention rather than repairing memory after amnesia.
change_log.reason: Within-animal reversibility of an enhancement is scientifically distinct from selective impairment-and-restoration.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include residual-information assessment, recovery without relearning, performance controls and separate validation of decoding.
change_log.reason: Behavioral improvement alone cannot establish persistence of original information, content-specific repair or complete physical identification.

change_log.change: Preserved conditional scientific and therapeutic significance while distinguishing inaccessible information from destroyed information.
change_log.reason: Selective recovery could be consequential without implying reconstruction of lost information or broad treatment of dementia.

change_log.change: Integrated evidence-access limitations and the missing freshness assessment.
change_log.reason: Complete text extraction does not equal independent inspection of figures, raw data or statistical tables, and source retrieval does not establish a current field survey.

change_log.reason: Shared methods and possible enabling roles do not justify merging separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish field-wide capabilities as of 1 November 2026; newer work and independent replication remain unassessed.
The full scope of the original assertions about distributed, changing and shared memory representations is not independently supported by the reviewed source.

The reviewed experiment does not establish direct assessment of surviving memory-specific information, arbitrary-content decoding, complete physical-trace identification or selective restoration after a defined impairment.
Figures, raw data and linked statistical tables were not independently inspected in the supplied review; effect magnitudes and robustness cannot be independently resolved from this record.

The proposed demonstrations still require operational definitions of residual information, sufficient trace identification, durability and acceptable unintended effects. No consensus thresholds are supplied.
Human translation and the extent to which selective restoration could help particular disease-related impairments remain unresolved.

brief.title: Reading and restoring specific memories
possible: People could recover a particular memory they can no longer recall, without learning it again and while preserving other tested memories. Researchers could locate its physical trace in the brain, identify what information it holds and determine whether that information survives the impairment.
why: For people with memory deficits, this could make inaccessible information recoverable and support treatment aimed at a particular lost memory. For scientists, it would connect specific information to the brain mechanisms that store it and control access to it.

sources.who: Davide M. Coda, Johannes Gräff and colleagues
sources.showed: In male mice, changing molecular controls on a gene in cells associated with learning strengthened or weakened learned fear responses. Researchers also reversed the enhancement within the same animals.
sources.quote:
Such effects occurred irrespective of the 
memory phase—during the initially labile period after learning and  
for fully consolidated memories—and were reversible within subject, 
testifying to their inherent plasticity.
sources.cited_for: Targeted molecular changes in memory-associated cells can causally alter learned behavior.
sources.not_established: Reversing an enhancement did not demonstrate repair of an impaired memory or identify its stored content.

sources.who: Tomás J. Ryan, Susumu Tonegawa and colleagues
sources.showed: Mice with drug-induced memory loss retrieved a learned fear response when light activated cells tagged during learning. Connections between memory-associated cells persisted despite the impairment.
sources.quote: direct optogenetic activation of these cells results in memory retrieval, and this correlates with the retained engram cell-specific connectivity.
sources.cited_for: Failure to recall a memory can occur while information needed for retrieval remains in the brain.
sources.not_established: Restoring a fear response did not decode the memory or establish lasting recovery through ordinary recall.

sources.who: Kareem Abdou, Kaoru Inokuchi and colleagues
sources.showed: Changing the strength of connections between brain cells selectively impaired a learned fear response while sparing another. Strengthening targeted connections also restored a tone-specific response after drug-induced memory loss.
sources.cited_for: Specific connections can help distinguish memories that share brain cells and can support selective recovery.
sources.not_established: Selective effects on tested fear memories did not establish preservation of all other memories or complete reading of their content.

sources.who: Adithya Sarma, Robbert Havekes and colleagues
sources.showed: After sleep deprivation disrupted mice's social recognition memories, activating cells tagged during particular encounters with light restored access and enabled selective retrieval.
sources.quote: Optogenetic reactivation of dentate gyrus engram cells restores social memory access and enables selective retrieval of individual memories.
sources.cited_for: Access to individual social memories can survive sleep deprivation and be selectively restored in mice.
sources.not_established: The experiments did not establish durable restoration of documented human memories or recovery of destroyed information.

shown: Adithya Sarma and colleagues restored access to particular social memories in sleep-deprived mice by using light to activate brain cells tagged during the encounters. This extends recovery beyond learned fear responses to recognition of other mice.

Kareem Abdou and colleagues selectively changed fear memories by altering connections between brain cells. Davide M. Coda and colleagues reversibly changed memory-related behavior through targeted molecular controls. These results demonstrate control over retrieval and behavior, rather than a complete reading of a memory.
missing: A combined demonstration must identify a specified memory's physical trace, measure surviving information and restore access without relearning.
Recovery must last while preserving other tested memories and avoiding general changes in attention, motivation or performance.
Human experiments must recover independently documented memories with precise targeting and measured unintended effects.

milestones.label: Replicated animal recovery of original information without relearning
milestones.explanation: Independent animal experiments would have to locate a specified memory's trace, assess surviving information after impairment and restore retrieval without relearning. This would distinguish recovery from new learning or better task performance.

milestones.label: Durable recovery that preserves other tested memories
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show lasting benefit, preserve comparison memories and measure other performance and unintended effects under stated conditions. This would establish selectivity within the tested set.

milestones.label: Physical features tied to specific memory information
milestones.explanation: Evidence would have to link physical features to specific learned content and distinguish a useful part of the trace from its complete representation. This would establish what researchers can actually read.

milestones.label: Durable recovery of documented human memories
milestones.explanation: Consenting participants would have to recover independently documented memories in blinded tests, with lasting benefit and controls for general performance changes. This would test human recovery, precision and unintended effects.

uncertain: How much original information must survive for a particular memory to be recoverable?
What counts as sufficient identification of a physical trace, lasting benefit and acceptable unintended effects?
Which disease-related impairments could selective restoration help? Recovering selected memories would not itself treat dementia broadly.

page.title: Memory engram decoding and selective memory restoration
page.definition: Neural measurements reveal retained content of a specified human episodic memory, a memory of an experienced event, after recall fails. An intervention targeted to its engram—the physical changes supporting that memory—restores access without relearning while preserving other tested memories.

goal.need: WHO estimates that 57 million people lived with dementia in 2021 and lists forgetting recent events among its early symptoms. This burden motivates memory-restoration research, but the population count does not measure recoverable memories or establish eligibility for an engram intervention.

statements.body: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), Restoring Active Memory programme
statements.quote: a fully implantable, closed-loop neural interface capable of restoring normal memory function
statements.context: The programme targets memory dysfunction following brain injury or illness.

statements.body: Wake Forest–University of Southern California hippocampal-prosthesis team
statements.quote: a future implantable neural prosthetic to improve human memory.

completion.title: A human experiment decodes retained episodic content and selectively restores its recall.
completion.criterion: In people with impaired recall of documented events, neural measurements predict event-specific content above task-specific chance on held-out tests while behavioral recall fails. An intervention directed at the identified trace then restores correct recall of that content without teaching it again. Controls distinguish recovery from new learning, cue leakage and general performance improvement; measured recall of tested comparison memories is preserved. The demonstration concerns the documented content and impairment tested.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no external completion criterion found for the combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of DARPA RAM goals, NIH BRAIN roadmaps, FDA neurostimulation material, ClinicalTrials.gov and published engram criteria found no test combining decoding during impaired recall with selective human restoration. RAM specifies restoration of memory function; engram criteria specify causal involvement in retrieval. The Atlas therefore uses their narrow integration for documented event content, without adding an unsupported effect size or durability threshold.

milestones.title: Activating a learning-tagged neuronal ensemble elicits recall without the original sensory cue.
milestones.criterion: Direct activation of learning-tagged neurons elicits the learned response without natural sensory retrieval cues; complementary loss-of-function tests impair recall when engram function is disrupted. These identify causal components of a trace. On 29 October 2025, Coda et al. additionally reported reversible molecular regulation of contextual fear expression: inducing an anti-CRISPR protein reversed enhancement in 8 male mice, compared with 7 controls. This was reversal of enhancement, not recovery after amnesia.
milestones.set_by: Participants in the Royal Society meeting on memory reactivation; Genzel et al. (2020), Box 1. This is a meeting-participant consensus, supplemented by Josselyn and Tonegawa's rodent causal tests.
milestones.threshold_quote: cell assembly coactivated during an animal experience and whose activation is sufficient to recall, in part, that experience

milestones.title: Direct activation of a tagged engram restores learned recall after experimentally induced amnesia.
milestones.criterion: After an impairment reduces cue-evoked recall, direct activation of learning-tagged neurons evokes the learned response without retraining. Ryan et al., published on 28 May 2015, demonstrated light-evoked freezing 2 days after training in anisomycin-treated mice: 8 treated mice and 10 saline controls, plus 4 no-shock controls per treatment. Cue-evoked impairment remained on day 3; artificial retrieval alone did not restore ordinary cue access.
milestones.set_by: Engram research community; retained-but-inaccessible memory test used by Ryan et al. (2015) and discussed by Josselyn and Tonegawa (2020). Published experiment used mouse contextual fear memory.
milestones.threshold_quote: direct optogenetic activation of these cells results in memory retrieval

milestones.title: Targeted engram intervention selectively retrieves one of two learned memories.
milestones.criterion: Tag one of two experiences and restore differential recall of the tagged experience. Sarma et al., published on 10 June 2026, tested two social encounters 48 hours apart, each followed by 6 hours of sleep deprivation: 12 male mice per tagging group preferentially explored the untagged mouse after stimulation. Abdou et al. reported increased 7-kHz-tone freezing after synaptic potentiation, with 2-kHz responses unaffected, in 10 mice per group, on 15 June 2018. Unchanged impaired recall does not establish preservation of an intact comparison memory.
milestones.set_by: Engram research community; memory-specific causal intervention, as explicitly tested by Sarma et al. (2026), Figure 4, and Abdou et al. (2018), Figure 4. These published tests concern mouse social and fear memories.
milestones.threshold_quote: optogenetic activation would selectively retrieve the tagged memory resulting in the test mice exploring the untagged stimulus mouse more than the tagged one.

milestones.title: Human hippocampal activity identifies which of 3 episodes is recalled above the 1/3 chance level.
milestones.criterion: Classify which of 3 previously viewed, 7-second film episodes a participant recalls from hippocampal functional MRI patterns, with performance significantly above chance. Chadwick et al., published online on 11 March 2010, reported decoding in 10 healthy adults, 6 female and 4 male. Figure 2 labels chance as 0.33. This discriminates known episodes; it does not reconstruct their full content or test impaired recall.
milestones.set_by: Human memory-decoding research convention of above-chance classification; three-episode implementation in Chadwick et al. (2010), Figure 2. The number of episodes is study-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: the dashed line at 0.33 represents chance-level performance.

milestones.title: Content-specific hippocampal stimulation improves human recognition of a target image category.
milestones.criterion: Stimulation derived from an image-category neural model improves delayed recognition against no-stimulation trials in the published task. Roeder et al., published on 8 February 2024, tested 14 epilepsy patients and reported significant changes in 22.4% of participant–category combinations, including improvements and impairments. Stimulation was delivered during encoding; the experiment did not retrieve an inaccessible pre-existing memory.
milestones.set_by: Memory-prosthesis research convention of stimulation-versus-control memory testing; category-specific delayed-recognition implementation in Roeder et al. (2024), sections 2.7.2 and 3.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Match Stim performance exceeded NoStim performance.

milestones.title: Targeted neural intervention restores documented human episodic recall without relearning.
milestones.criterion: A controlled human intervention restores correct recall of independently documented, previously inaccessible event content without supplying that content again. The effect is specific to the targeted memory, with measured recall of comparison memories preserved against controls. This establishes selective behavioral recovery; decoding retained information from the trace before intervention remains a separate requirement for completion.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of DARPA RAM material, memory-prosthesis studies and ClinicalTrials.gov found no published criterion for selective recovery of documented human memories without relearning.

not_found: No external test was found for combined decoding of retained content and selective restoration of an inaccessible human memory.
No accepted numerical thresholds were found for content fidelity, durability or preservation of comparison memories in this combined capability.
ClinicalTrials.gov searches did not locate a human protocol with the combined decoding-and-restoration endpoint.
The supplied Nature publisher page and AAAS collection PDF were inaccessible; readable copies of both papers were found on ResearchGate.

results.finding: In male mice, anti-CRISPR induction reversed enhanced fear-memory retention in 8 treated animals versus 7 controls.
results.detail: The intervention regulated a learning-tagged ensemble, but recall was tested with the conditioned context. It did not elicit recall without a natural retrieval cue.
results.quote:
Compared to animals expressing dCas9-VPR plus 
Arc sgRNA and kept off DOX (n = 7), animals put ON DOX after the first recall 
to induce AcrIIA4 (n = 8) showed impaired memory retention

results.finding: Light activation of tagged CA1 cells elicited freezing in 9 anisomycin-treated mice and 10 saline controls; p < 0.001 for the treated group.
results.detail: The paper reports activation-induced recall without the original context cue. It discusses complementary loss-of-function recall tests as previous studies, rather than reporting them as a result of this experiment.
results.quote: 1 day post-CFC (Test 1) ANI group (n = 9) displayed significantly less freezing than SAL group (n = 10) in Context B (p < 0.01). 2 days post-training (Engram Activation), light-activation of CA1 engrams elicited freezing in both SAL (p < 0.01) and ANI groups (p < 0.001).

results.finding: Light activation elicited freezing after amnesia in 9 anisomycin-treated mice versus 10 saline controls; p < 0.001 in the treated group.
results.detail: Cue-evoked freezing was impaired before stimulation and remained impaired on the following day. Light activation evoked recall without retraining.
results.quote: 1 day post-CFC (Test 1) ANI group (n = 9) displayed significantly less freezing than SAL group (n = 10) in Context B (p < 0.01). 2 days post-training (Engram Activation), light-activation of CA1 engrams elicited freezing in both SAL (p < 0.01) and ANI groups (p < 0.001).

results.finding: In mice, activation of neurons tagged during 7-kHz fear conditioning elicited recall; sample size not stated.
results.detail: Optical activation elicited recall without the tone, but the reported drug-induced impairment did not selectively disrupt the tagged ensemble.
results.quote:
Optogenetic activation of the axonal terminals of the AC and MGm engram cells in the LA induced
fear memory recall in the PBS and anisomycin
groups, which is consistent with a previous study
(21), whereas it failed to do this in the Ani+tBC-
treated mice (Fig. 1F).

results.finding: In anisomycin-treated mice, direct activation of the 7-kHz learning-tagged ensemble elicited fear recall; sample size not stated.
results.detail: Anisomycin induced partial retrograde amnesia; optical activation elicited recall without retraining.

results.finding: In anisomycin-treated mice, synaptic potentiation restored freezing to the 7-kHz conditioned tone; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The comparison was a neutral 2-kHz tone, rather than a second learned fear memory in the recovery experiment.
results.quote:
Optical
LTP allowed anisomycin-treated mice to com-
pletely recover from amnesia to the PBS group’s
freezing level, which was specific to the 7-kHz
conditioned tone (i.e., it did not generalize to the
2-kHz tone) (Fig. 1G).

results.finding: In sleep-deprived mice, tagged-ensemble activation restored social recognition; 9 to 12 mice per group were tested.
results.detail: The learned response was measured when the mice were reexposed to the social stimuli. The study did not demonstrate recall without the original sensory cues or report a complementary engram loss-of-function test.
results.quote: In contrast, the sleep-deprived mice that underwent optogenetic reactivation of DG engram cells explored both the stimulus mouse and the cagemate equally, showing successful retrieval of the previously formed social memory

results.finding: Tagged-ensemble activation restored social recognition after sleep deprivation in groups of 9 to 12 mice.
results.detail: Stimulation preceded the test, which reexposed mice to the original social stimuli. The result supports recovery of cue-tested recognition without retraining, but does not show that activation alone evoked the learned response.
results.quote: Five to 10 min before the memory test, the memory engram was optogenetically reactivated in one group of mice, while the other group was tethered to the cable without stimulation.

results.finding: In 12 mice per tagging group, stimulation produced preferential exploration of the untagged social stimulus.
results.detail: The two social experiences were 48 hours apart and each was followed by sleep deprivation. The untagged memory was also impaired, so this does not establish preservation of an intact comparison memory.
results.quote: In the social memory test, both groups explored the untagged stimulus mouse significantly more than the tagged one, aligning with our third predicted outcome

results.finding: In male mice, activating learning-tagged CA1 neurons elicited fear-memory recall in a neutral context (11 per group; p=0.0004).
results.detail: Inhibiting CA1 engram cells reduced recall in the training context (11 mice per group; p=0.0002).
results.quote:
As a positive control, we observed robust memory recall by the optogenetic reactivation of dorsal CA1 engram cells at 4 Hz specifically (Fig.
4c
and Supplementary Fig.
3a
), as well as by the reactivation of BLA engram cells at both 4 and 20 Hz frequencies (Fig.
4d
and Supplementary Fig.

).

results.finding: In 12 anisomycin-treated and 10 control mice, engram activation evoked freezing 2 days after training.
results.detail: Anisomycin reduced natural cue-evoked recall on day 1. Both groups froze during light-on epochs without retraining; the treated group remained amnesic to natural cues the next day.

results.finding: Early Alzheimer’s-model mice (9 per group) froze when learning-tagged engram cells were activated 2 days after training.
results.detail: Natural cue recall was impaired one day after training and remained impaired on day 3 after light activation. The impairment arose in a transgenic Alzheimer’s model, rather than from anisomycin treatment.
results.quote: But, remarkably, these mice froze on the next day in a distinct context (Context B) as robustly as equivalently treated control mice in response to blue light stimulation of the engram cells

results.finding: In 10 healthy adults, hippocampal fMRI classified recalled film episodes significantly above the 0.33 chance level.
results.detail: Participants recalled three previously viewed, 7-second films. Reported results pooled cued and free recall trials; decoding does not establish full content reconstruction or recovery from impaired recall.
results.quote: Proportion accuracy values are shown on the vertical axis; the dashed line at 0.33 represents chance-level performance. All three areas were significantly above chance-level performance, with hippocampus (HC) accuracy significantly greater than both entorhinal cortex (EC) and parahippocampal gyrus (PHG)

results.finding: In 14 epilepsy patients, category-matched stimulation significantly improved delayed recognition in 9 of 67 patient–category combinations.
results.detail: Five combinations showed significant decreases. Stimulation was delivered during encoding, and estimated statistical power was approximately 10% per patient–category and stimulation-type combination.
results.quote: Thus, 13.4% of the time MDM stimulation resulted in significantly facilitated performance relative to NoStim.
